finalResponse:
# Health-Feature Strategy Under Divergent Regulatory Classification
## "One algorithm, one evidence base, three claim tiers, many jurisdictions"

---

## 1. Diagnose correctly: classification is one of four dials, and it is not the binding one

The instinct is to treat this as a regulatory-affairs sequencing problem — file where you can, ship "wellness" where you can't. That solves the least important constraint and creates the most damaging failure mode: a product that says different things about the same physiology in different countries, with no defensible reason why.

| Dial | What actually varies by market | Wrong response | Right response |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Claim** (what you're allowed to say) | MDR Rule 11 in the EU, PMD Act "program medical device" in Japan, pending US classification, wellness carve-outs elsewhere | Maximize the claim each regulator permits | Claim is capped by the **global evidence dossier**, then further capped by local law |
| **Evidence** (what you can prove) | Nothing — physiology is global; only *acceptance* of evidence varies (Japanese-subject data, EU clinical evaluation, FDA subgroup expectations) | Run a study per jurisdiction | One **union-designed pivotal study** + modular dossier serving all filings |
| **Care pathway** (what happens after a flag) | Sleep-lab and HSAT capacity, specialist density, referral culture, out-of-pocket diagnostic cost | Ship the flag; downstream is the user's problem | **Pathway-readiness gate**: no screening claim without a route to confirmation |
| **Trust** (who must vouch for it) | Physician-mediated in Japan, institution/privacy-mediated in the EU, brand/peer-mediated in emerging markets | One global "clinically validated" campaign | Region-specific credibility architecture; same evidence, different validators |

**Core insight:** regulatory classification determines *what you may say*, but the **care pathway determines whether saying it creates value or harm**, and the **evidence dossier determines whether the claim survives contact with a skeptical sleep-medicine community.** A wellness-classified market where 4% of flagged users can actually obtain a diagnostic test is a worse launch than a delayed medical-device market. Classification is the third-most-important variable.

**Second insight, for the pipeline question:** clinical evidence, QMS maturity, notified-body relationships, and an authorized change-control plan are **largely fixed, reusable assets**. The first feature is expensive because it builds the factory; features two through six should be underwritten on **marginal evidence cost**, not fully-allocated program cost. The strategic objective for sleep apnea is therefore not sleep apnea revenue — it is to **build a regulatory flywheel that makes the next five features 3–5× cheaper and 12 months faster.**

---

## 2. Global invariants vs. the localizable layer

**Invariants (identical everywhere, non-negotiable):**

- **One algorithm, one version, one performance profile.** No market gets a degraded or "unregulated-lite" model. Divergence is in *labeling and output granularity*, never in the sensing or inference stack.
- **One evidence dossier of record**, structured to IMDRF Table-of-Contents so EU, US, Japan, and reliance-pathway filings draw from the same modules.
- **The Evidence Floor** (§3.2): no market receives a claim the global dossier cannot support — *even if the local regulator would permit it*. Regulatory permission is a floor, not a license.
- **One QMS** (ISO 13485 / IEC 62304 / ISO 14971 / IEC 62366) applied to the feature globally, including in wellness markets where it isn't required.
- **Subgroup performance parity commitment**: published sensitivity/specificity by skin tone, BMI band, sex, and age decile. Any subgroup falling below a pre-declared threshold suppresses the feature for that subgroup globally, not locally.
- **One adverse-event and complaint pipeline**, ingesting wellness-market signals into the same vigilance system as regulated markets.

**Configurable per market (the "Market Claim Profile"):**
Claim tier and exact notification wording; output granularity (categorical risk vs. numeric index); frequency of notification; localized IFU and human-factors-validated language; referral partner and in-app care pathway; clinician-facing artifacts; consumer evidence-communication style; data residency configuration; whether the feature is on by default or opt-in.

**Rule:** a market gets a new **Claim Profile**, never a new algorithm and never a claim outside the global taxonomy. Any request for a market-specific claim construct goes to the Claims Council (§9).

---

## 3. Claim architecture: three tiers, one ladder

### 3.1 The tier taxonomy

| Tier | Language pattern | Output shown | Typical classification | Evidence required |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **T0 — Wellness** | "Breathing disturbances during sleep," trends over time | Relative trend only; no threshold, no "apnea," no risk verdict | General wellness / unregulated | Analytical validation + non-misleading UX comprehension testing |
| **T1 — Screening / case-finding** | "Signs consistent with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea. This is not a diagnosis — see a clinician." | Binary or 3-band risk flag over a defined observation window | EU MDR Class IIa; Japan Class II program device; US 510(k)/De Novo | Pivotal PSG-referenced study; subgroup analysis; PMS/PMCF plan |
| **T2 — Diagnostic-adjacent / monitoring** | Quantified index, therapy-response tracking, clinician-reportable | Numeric AHI-analogue, longitudinal report | Higher class; possibly clinician-prescribed | Outcomes evidence, clinical utility, human-factors for clinician use |

The 2026 launch is a **T1 program with a T0 fallback**. T2 is a 2028+ ambition that shapes study design today (endpoints designed in are cheap; retrofitted are not).

### 3.2 The Evidence Floor — the rule that protects the whole program

```
Permitted claim in market M = MIN(
    claim supported by global evidence dossier,
    claim permitted by M's regulator,
    claim supported by M's care-pathway readiness score,
    claim validated for comprehension in M's language/health-literacy context
)
```

If a market can't reach T1 on any of the four terms, **you do not weaken the claim's evidence — you drop the tier**. T0 is always available and always honest. This is the discipline that prevents the classic failure: a "wellness" launch in a permissive market that markets itself as diagnostic, generates a viral false-positive story, and poisons the EU and Japan filings that are still under review.

**Corollary:** because T0 markets run the same algorithm and same QMS, they are not a compliance liability — they are **the largest real-world evidence generator you will ever own**, and their data feeds PMCF for the regulated markets.

---

## 4. The evidence engine

### 4.1 One pivotal study, designed to the union of requirements

Do not run three studies. Run one prospective, multi-site, PSG-referenced pivotal study designed to the **superset** of EU MDR clinical evaluation, FDA, and PMDA expectations:

- **Sites:** US (3–4), EU (2–3, including one Germany or Nordics for MDR credibility), **Japan (2 sites, ~15–20% of enrollment)** — pre-planned Japanese subgroup consistency analysis is the single highest-leverage design decision, converting a probable PMDA bridging demand into an already-answered question.
- **Enrollment:** ~1,000–1,500 completing simultaneous device + attended PSG, enriched across AHI strata so the moderate-to-severe boundary is precisely characterized.
- **Powered subgroups:** Fitzpatrick V–VI, BMI ≥35 and <25, female (historically under-enrolled in sleep research — a differentiator, not just a compliance item), age ≥65, and comorbid arrhythmia.
- **Endpoints:** primary sensitivity/specificity at the moderate-to-severe threshold; secondary PPV/NPV modeled at *real-world* population prevalence (this is what clinicians will attack — pre-empt it); plus **pre-specified clinical-utility endpoints** (referral completion, diagnostic confirmation rate, therapy initiation at 90 days) that cost little now and unlock reimbursement conversations later.
- **Indicative cost:** $10–16M, ~14–18 months. Treat as platform capex, not feature opex.

### 4.2 The evidence ladder, and where money goes

| Layer | Purpose | Reuse across pipeline |
|---|---|---|
| Analytical / bench validation | Sensor-to-signal accuracy, robustness to motion, wear position, ambient conditions | Very high — sensor-level, reused by all features |
| Pivotal clinical validation | The regulatory claim | Low — feature-specific |
| Human-factors & comprehension | Users act correctly on the notification; required by FDA/IEC 62366, and the thing most often failed | High — notification framework reused |
| Real-world performance registry | PMCF, drift detection, subgroup surveillance, T0-market learning | Very high — one registry, all features |
| Clinical utility / outcomes | Society endorsement, guidelines, reimbursement | Medium |
| Health-economic modeling | Payer and public-health entry (DiGA, NICE, Japanese reimbursement) | Medium |

**Budget rule:** roughly 55% pivotal, 20% real-world registry infrastructure, 15% human factors and localization/comprehension, 10% outcomes/health-economics. Underfunding comprehension testing is the most common and most expensive mistake — a notification that 30% of users read as a diagnosis is a regulatory event in every jurisdiction simultaneously.

### 4.3 Build the change-control plan before you need it

The defining architectural bet: pursue an authorized **Predetermined Change Control Plan** with FDA and the equivalent pre-agreed change-management framework with the EU notified body and PMDA, specifying in advance which algorithm modifications (retraining on new data, threshold tuning within bounds, new device hardware within a defined sensor-equivalence envelope) can ship without a new submission.

Without this, every model improvement is an 8–14 month regulatory event and the product ossifies. With it, you get consumer-electronics iteration speed inside a medical-device wrapper. **Design the ML lifecycle, data governance, and performance-monitoring telemetry around the PCCP from day one** — retrofitting it is nearly impossible.

---

## 5. Sequencing: gate by evidence readiness, not by geography

Markets don't queue behind each other; they queue behind **gates**. Run four waves in parallel where gates permit.

| Wave | Markets | Tier | Gate that must clear | Indicative timing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0 — Learn** | 4–6 wellness-classified emerging markets (selected for scale + data quality, not permissiveness) | **T0 only** | Algorithm frozen; QMS in place; comprehension testing done in local languages; explicit "not a diagnosis" UX | T0 → launch at T+0 |
| **1 — Anchor** | US | **T1** | Pivotal readout; classification resolved; predicates now exist in-category, so target the shortest authorized route with a PCCP attached | Submit T+16, live T+22–26 |
| **2 — Depth** | EU (MDR IIa) + Japan (Class II) | **T1** | Same dossier; notified-body slot **booked at T+2, not T+16** — capacity is the true critical path; Japan filed within 6 months of EU using the pre-planned Japanese subgroup | EU live T+26–32; Japan T+28–34 |
